[THOUGHT]  
The patient is a 55-year-old male with progressive, purely motor, right arm weakness over weeks—no sensory symptoms, no cranial nerve, brainstem, cerebellar, or gait involvement. This localizes the lesion to the *motor pathway* from anterior horn cell (or proximal nerve root) distally through peripheral nerve/muscle—but critically *spares sensation*, making central (e.g., cortical/subcortical stroke) and most radicular or plexal lesions *less likely unless they are highly selective for motor fibers*. However, pure motor radiculopathy (e.g., C6/C7) is rare but possible; more commonly, radiculopathy includes sensory symptoms. The absence of trauma, cancer, autoimmune disease, or repetitive strain reduces likelihood of traumatic plexopathy, malignancy-related brachial plexopathy, or inflammatory plexitis (e.g., neuralgic amyotrophy), though not excluded. Diabetes is present—but duration, control, and HbA1c are unknown; diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy (e.g., diabetic amyotrophy) typically affects *lower limbs* (lumbosacral plexus); upper-limb–predominant diabetic mononeuropathy is exceedingly rare and usually acute, focal, and self-limited (e.g., radial or axillary mononeuropathy), not progressive over weeks. Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) fits *exceptionally well*: it is an immune-mediated, purely motor, asymmetric, progressive neuropathy that often begins in one upper limb, causes weakness (e.g., wrist/finger drop), has no sensory findings, spares bulbar and respiratory function, and may show conduction block on EMG—though anti-GM1 antibodies are only positive in ~50%. It occurs in middle-aged adults, lacks systemic inflammation (ESR/CRP normal expected), and is not associated with diabetes or other systemic illness. Cervical radiculopathy remains plausible—but the *absence of pain, sensory changes, or reflex asymmetry* (not stated, but if present would likely have been noted given focused neuro exam) makes it less compelling than MMN. Brachial plexopathy would typically cause more diffuse or multi-root involvement and often includes some sensory or pain features. Central lesion is strongly disfavored: no UMN signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski), no contralateral or additional neurological deficits, and progression over weeks is atypical for most acute/subacute corticospinal lesions (e.g., tumor or demyelination would likely show other signs on exam or imaging). Thus, MMN is the *most specific diagnosis* that explains the full clinical picture: insidious, asymmetric, purely motor, upper-limb–predominant, progressive weakness in a middle-aged adult without red flags for structural or systemic disease.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive right arm weakness over several weeks  
- Purely motor presentation: no numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in right arm/hand  
- No cranial nerve, brainstem, cerebellar, or gait abnormalities  
- No history of trauma, cancer, autoimmune disease, or prior neurological disorders  
- Normal CBC (no evidence of systemic infection, hematologic malignancy, or inflammation)  
- Age (55 years) falls within typical MMN onset range (30–70 years)  
- Asymmetric distribution (right arm only) — hallmark of MMN  
- Functional impairment (e.g., dropping objects) consistent with distal > proximal motor involvement common in MMN  

[GAPS]  
- Nerve conduction study (NCS) and EMG results — required to detect conduction block (diagnostic for MMN) or alternative patterns (e.g., denervation without block in radiculopathy/plexopathy)  
- Anti-GM1 IgM antibody status — supportive (though not required) for MMN diagnosis  
- Cervical spine MRI — needed to definitively exclude compressive radiculopathy or plexopathy  
- Serum creatine kinase (CK) — to assess for myopathic contribution (not mentioned, but normal in MMN)  
- Detailed motor exam findings (e.g., pattern of weakness — wrist/finger extension vs. shoulder abduction; presence/absence of fasciculations or atrophy) — not specified  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Multifocal motor neuropathy

The patient is a 55-year-old male with progressive right arm weakness over several weeks and functional impairment (e.g., dropping objects). Critically, there are *no sensory symptoms* in the right arm/hand, and no cranial nerve, brainstem, cerebellar, or gait abnormalities — meaning the deficit is isolated to motor function in the right upper limb. No trauma, cancer, autoimmune disease, or prior neurological disorders are reported. CBC is normal, ruling out overt hematologic or infectious systemic illness. Diabetes is present but uncharacterized (no HbA1c, glucose, or control data), so its contribution remains uncertain but unconfirmed. Among the differential, cervical radiculopathy is plausible anatomically (C6/C7 roots supply arm flexors/extensors) but classically presents with pain and often sensory changes — neither is reported. Brachial plexopathy typically causes more widespread or multi-level weakness and frequently includes pain or some sensory involvement; absence of both makes it less likely without corroborating imaging or EMG. Compressive neuropathies (e.g., radial nerve) usually produce a stereotyped pattern (e.g., wrist drop) — but the summary does not specify *which muscles or movements are weak*, only that functional impairment includes “dropping objects”, which implies impaired grip or finger/wrist extension — yet this detail alone is insufficient to localize. Diabetic mononeuropathy affecting upper limb is exceptionally rare and typically acute and monofocal (e.g., sudden wrist drop), not subacute progressive. Central lesions (e.g., corticospinal tract) are strongly disfavored: no UMN signs (e.g., spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski), no contralateral findings, no dysarthria/visual/gait issues — and progression over weeks is atypical for most focal CNS lesions (e.g., tumor or stroke would usually be static or rapidly progressive, not insidiously worsening over weeks without other signs). Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) remains the *most parsimonious diagnosis* that fits all *explicitly stated facts*: (1) asymmetric, purely motor, progressive upper-limb weakness; (2) no sensory involvement; (3) no systemic illness or red flags; (4) age-appropriate; (5) no alternative explanation confirmed by available data. While MMN is rare, it is the *only diagnosis in the provided differential* that routinely presents with *isolated, progressive, asymmetric motor weakness without sensory loss, pain, or systemic features*, and it cannot be excluded without EMG/NCS — which is pending.
